title: The 10 Best Pneumatic Brad Nailers
subtitle: 18-gauge air brad nailers for trim, molding and furniture, ranked from live Amazon data.
intro: A pneumatic brad nailer drives thin 18-gauge brads, 5/8 to 2 inches long, for trim, baseboard, casing and furniture. It needs an air compressor, but even a small pancake runs one, and it's lighter and much cheaper than a cordless model. We ranked 10 best-sellers on rating, review volume and features (tool-free depth adjustment, tool-free jam release, oil-free motor, selectable trigger and a case). They run from about $29 for a bare NuMax to $134 for Makita's aluminum AF506. See our air compressor list if you need one.

changelog.note: Page published with 10 ranked picks and 1 tool to avoid.

products.name: BOSTITCH Brad Nailer Kit, 18GA, Smart Point, Pneumatic (BTFP12233)

specs.in_box: Case, air fitting, extra no-mar tips

cons: The listing's 5.16 lb weight looks like the boxed kit, so check the tool weight elsewhere

avoid.name: NuMax SL31 Pneumatic 3-in-1 Nail Gun, 16 GA & 18 GA Finish Nailer, Brad Nailer, Stapler
avoid.flag: One magazine for 16 ga nails, 18 ga brads and staples
avoid.verdict: A 3-in-1 gun that tries to drive two nail gauges and staples through one nose. Buy a dedicated 18-gauge nailer here, or a separate 16-gauge finish nailer if you need one.
reasons: It claims to fire 16-gauge finish nails, 18-gauge brads and 18-gauge staples. 16- and 18-gauge fasteners are different thicknesses; one drive blade and nose sized for both fit neither perfectly, which is how jams and bent nails happen.
It's rated 4.1 stars, the lowest of any brad nailer we considered with this many reviews.
For about $18 less, NuMax's own SBR50 does the 18-gauge job with a dedicated mechanism, and the $40 NEU MASTER 2-in-1 adds staples.

buyers_guide.a: An 18-gauge brad nailer shoots thin nails that leave tiny holes, ideal for trim, casing and small molding. A 16-gauge finish nailer shoots thicker, longer nails for baseboard, door jambs and heavier trim. Most people start with a brad nailer.

buyers_guide.q: What size compressor do I need?
buyers_guide.a: Brad nailers use very little air, well under 1 CFM. Any pancake or small hot-dog compressor runs one easily. See our air compressor list.
Oil-free nailers don't need a few drops of oil each day and won't spit oil onto finished wood. Oiled nailers are fine for paint-grade trim; keep a rag handy.

Sequential (single) mode fires one nail per trigger pull with the nose pressed: safer and more precise. Bump (contact) mode fires each time the nose touches with the trigger held, which is faster for repetitive work. A selectable trigger gives you both.

If you'll staple upholstery, drawer bottoms or screen as well as nail trim, yes. Brads and 1/4-inch narrow crown staples share a magazine width, so the combo tools work well. Avoid tools that also claim 16-gauge nails.
